approaches.name: Pediatric lateral-trochanteric entry for rigid femoral nailing
approaches.corridor: Longitudinal lateral fascia-lata split to a start lateral and inferior to the greater-trochanter tip, collinear with the canal on the lateral view

sources.title: Entry Point For Lateral Entry Intramedullary Nailing
Advances in the surgical management of pediatric femoral shaft fractures
Treatment options in pediatric femoral shaft fractures

procedure_applications.condition: An older or heavier pediatric patient is selected for a pediatric lateral-entry locked nail, with sufficient canal size and open-growth-plate considerations addressed

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the proximal lateral femur accessible and the entire femur imageable in AP and lateral planes.

setup.text: Confirm skeletal maturity, trochanteric anatomy, canal size, fracture reduction strategy, and compatibility of the implant with a lateral entry before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the palpable greater-trochanter tip, anterior and posterior trochanter borders, femoral axis, and a lateral fluoroscopic projection of the canal.

incision.text: Center the incision on the trochanter tip, extending about 3 cm proximally and distally as required, in line with the medullary canal on the lateral image.

superficial_interval.text: Incise fascia lata longitudinally in the same direction and spread the underlying tissues to expose the lateral greater trochanter.

deep_interval.text: Palpate both trochanter borders and establish the nail entry lateral and inferior to the greater-trochanter tip under orthogonal fluoroscopy.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata, limited abductor-vastus soft-tissue corridor, trochanteric cortex, then femoral canal.

structures_encountered.text: Fascia lata, greater trochanter, abductor insertion region, proximal femoral cortex, and medullary canal define the approach.

structures_at_risk.text: The greater-trochanteric apophysis, abductor mechanism, proximal femoral cortex, femoral-neck blood supply, and posterior cortex are at risk from an incorrect portal or trajectory.

danger_zones.text: Avoid a piriformis-fossa portal in a skeletally immature patient and avoid medial, superior, anterior, or posterior deviation from the implant-specific lateral start.

retraction_hazards.text: Do not lever instruments against the trochanter or abductors to compensate for a poorly aligned incision; extend the skin and fascia until the working path is collinear.

exposure.text: Provides a physeal-conscious lateral portal for a compatible locked rigid nail without opening the shaft fracture.

limitations.text: Requires an adequately sized canal and a patient and fracture pattern appropriate for locked nailing; it is not interchangeable with piriformis-entry implant geometry.

extensions.text: Extend proximally or distally along the lateral incision to obtain a collinear track; use a separate limited reduction window only when closed reduction fails.

indications.text: Use in selected older, heavier children or adolescents with femoral-shaft fractures unsuitable for flexible nails and suitable for a lateral-entry locked nail.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid when patient size, open proximal femoral growth anatomy, canal diameter, fracture location, infection, or implant design prevents a safe lateral-entry construct.

implant_implications.text: Use only a nail designed for pediatric lateral-trochanteric entry; match diameter and curvature to the canal and keep guidewire, reamer, and nail on the planned axis.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm the portal lateral and inferior to the trochanter tip on AP view and collinear with the canal laterally, then monitor reduction, reaming, depth, and locking across the whole femur.

closure.text: Irrigate, obtain hemostasis, repair fascia lata without abductor tethering, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include growth disturbance, abductor injury, osteonecrosis, trochanteric or neck fracture, cortical perforation, malalignment, nonunion, infection, and hardware irritation.

bailouts.text: If the implant-specific safe start cannot be achieved, stop repeated opening attempts and change positioning, exposure, or fixation strategy rather than using a hazardous portal.

questions.question: Where is the rigid lateral-entry start?
questions.answer: On the lateral greater trochanter, lateral and inferior to its tip.

questions.question: How is the incision aligned?
questions.answer: With the medullary canal on the lateral fluoroscopic view.

questions.question: Why avoid piriformis entry in an immature patient?
questions.answer: It risks proximal femoral blood supply and growth-related complications; a compatible lateral-entry design is preferred.

approaches.name: Pediatric retrograde ESIN entry approaches to the femur
approaches.corridor: Paired medial and lateral distal-metaphyseal windows at the same level, 2–3 cm proximal to the distal femoral growth plate and centered sagittally

sources.title: ESIN Entry Points For Retrograde Nailing
Elastic Stable Intramedullary Nailing for Fractures in Children - Specific Applications
Femoral shaft fractures in children: elastic stable intramedullary nailing in 31 cases

procedure_applications.condition: A pediatric femoral-shaft fracture is suitable for paired retrograde elastic nails and safe distal metaphyseal entry above the open physis

positioning.text: Position supine with the knee and distal femur accessible and the full femur imageable on orthogonal views.

setup.text: Map the distal femoral physis, template two equal elastic nails and balanced curves, and ensure reduction and imaging from knee to hip.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the medial and lateral epicondyles, joint line, distal femoral physis under fluoroscopy, shaft center, and symmetric planned entry levels.

incision.text: Make separate approximately 3-cm medial and lateral incisions beginning at each entry and extending distally to permit oblique nail advancement.

superficial_interval.text: Spread fascia and muscle bluntly on each side to expose cortex while protecting medial neurovascular and lateral soft-tissue structures.

deep_interval.text: Create entries at the same axial level, 2–3 cm proximal to the growth plate, centered in the shaft on the sagittal plane and directed away from the physis.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, medial or lateral fascia and muscle, periosteum, distal metaphyseal cortex, then medullary canal.

structures_encountered.text: Distal femoral physis, medial and lateral metaphyseal cortex, vastus medialis and lateralis, periosteum, and canal are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: The distal femoral physis, saphenous nerve and vein medially, lateral soft tissues, cortex, knee capsule, and femoral vessels with uncontrolled medial passage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Entry closer than 2 cm to the physis risks growth injury; asymmetric, posterior, or closely placed portals risk cortical split, malalignment, or soft-tissue injury.

retraction_hazards.text: Use blunt dissection and protective sleeves to bone; avoid blind medial clamping, forceful nail-end levering, and soft-tissue entrapment around rotating nails.

exposure.text: Provides balanced paired retrograde access to the femoral canal while avoiding the hip and leaving the fracture zone closed.

limitations.text: Best suited to appropriately sized children and length-stable diaphyseal patterns; heavier children and unstable proximal or distal patterns have less reliable control.

extensions.text: Lengthen either incision for controlled cortical visualization rather than accepting an uncertain percutaneous portal or prominent nail end.

indications.text: Use for selected pediatric femoral-shaft fractures in children whose size, fracture stability, and canal can support balanced elastic fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Favor another construct for length-unstable patterns, very proximal or distal fractures, inadequate canal size, severe obesity, local infection, or inability to protect the physis.

implant_implications.text: Use two equal-diameter precontoured nails with opposing bends and symmetric entries; bury or trim ends to avoid knee and soft-tissue irritation without preventing removal.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm physeal distance and sagittal centering for both portals, then monitor canal passage, reduction, length, axes, rotation, and final nail-end position.

closure.text: Confirm hemostasis and nonprominent nail ends, release entrapped soft tissue, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin, preferably with absorbable sutures.

complications.text: Complications include physeal injury, cortical split, malalignment or shortening, nail migration, medial or lateral irritation, knee stiffness, infection, delayed union, and refracture.

bailouts.text: If a portal is unsafe or the fracture remains unstable after balanced nails, stop, revise the entry or reduction under direct vision, supplement fixation, or change constructs.

questions.question: How far proximal to the physis are retrograde ESIN entries?
Where are the entries on the sagittal plane?
questions.answer: In the middle of the femoral shaft.

questions.question: Why are the two portals placed at the same level?
questions.answer: To create balanced opposing elastic fixation and avoid asymmetric deforming forces.
